title: 'Arms and the man': the proem
greek: Arma virumque cano
short: The first words announce a poem of war ('arms', the Iliad) and of one man's journey ('the man', the Odyssey): Virgil sets himself against both Homeric epics at once.
body: Virgil's opening is a programme. 'Arms' recalls the Iliad, a poem of battle; 'the man' (virum) recalls the first word of the Odyssey, andra, 'the man of many turns'. Roughly speaking, Books 1-6 are Virgil's Odyssey (wandering) and Books 7-12 his Iliad (war in Italy). Unlike Homer, who asks the Muse to sing, Virgil says 'I sing' (cano), and he only calls on the Muse at 1.8. The sentence runs from Troy to Rome in seven lines, ending on 'the stately city Rome' (altae moenia Romae), so that the whole history of Rome is the goal of the story. Servius already noticed a difficulty in 'who first' (qui primus): Antenor reached Italy earlier (see 1.242), and Servius explains that Aeneas was first to reach Lavinium. The phrase arma virumque became so famous that, as Conington's note records, it has been found scribbled on the walls of Pompeii.

title: Fato profugus: exile driven by fate
greek: fato profugus
short: Aeneas is a refugee, but a refugee 'by fate': his flight is part of a divine plan that ends in Rome.
body: Profugus means a fugitive or exile, someone who has fled his home. Virgil joins it to fato, 'by fate' or 'by destiny', and the word fatum (literally 'what has been spoken', from fari, to speak) runs through the poem: the decree of Jupiter that Rome shall be founded. Conington suggests the force 'a fugitive indeed, but a fugitive by fate', a glorious and heaven-sent exile, and compares Livy's language for Aeneas led by fate 'to greater beginnings'. Page argues that fato goes as much with 'came' (venit) as with 'exile': the point is that destiny brought him to Italy. Mackail's 'exile of fate' keeps the ambiguity. Against fate stands Juno's anger (1.4), and the tension between the two drives Books 1-6: Juno can delay what is fated but cannot stop it (compare Jupiter at 1.257-96 and Juno's own admission at 7.313-16).

title: Lavinium
greek: Lavinaque ... litora
short: Lavinium, near the coast south of Rome, was the town Aeneas was said to have founded and named after his Latin wife Lavinia.
body: Lavinium (modern Pratica di Mare) lay about 30 km south of Rome. Roman tradition made it Aeneas' first city in Italy, named after Lavinia, daughter of King Latinus, whom he marries after the war of Books 7-12; it remained a religious centre where Roman magistrates sacrificed to the Penates (the household gods Aeneas brought from Troy). Jupiter's prophecy in this book traces the line Lavinium - Alba Longa - Rome (1.258-77). Virgil names it in line 2 by anticipation: the 'shore' is called Lavinian before there is any Lavinium. The manuscripts vary between Lavina and Lavinia; both Conington and Page accept Lavina, an adjective coined from the place name, and Page notes that the poets take freedoms with the quantities of proper names.

title: Pietas: Aeneas' 'goodness'
greek: insignem pietate virum
short: Mackail's 'goodness' renders pietas, the defining Roman virtue of dutiful loyalty to gods, family and country, and the source of Aeneas' standing epithet pius.
body: Pietas is not 'piety' in the modern, narrowly religious sense. It is the sense of duty owed to those to whom one is bound: the gods, parents and children, kin, and the fatherland. Page, in his note on 1.10, lists these and observes that Aeneas is 'pious' above all because he cared for the Penates and carried his father out of burning Troy. Mackail consistently translates pietas as 'goodness' and the epithet pius as 'good', so 'good Aeneas' (1.220, 1.305) and 'Aeneas the good' (1.378) all stand for pius Aeneas. The proem poses the poem's great question: why should a man so marked by pietas suffer so much at the hands of a goddess? Pietas also has an obligation running the other way: men who keep faith may expect justice from heaven, which is why Venus asks Jupiter 'Is this the reward of goodness?' (hic pietatis honos? 1.253).

anchor: anger so fierce in celestial spirits
title: The anger of Juno and the question of divine justice
greek: tantaene animis caelestibus irae?
short: The invocation ends in a question that the whole poem keeps asking: how can gods feel such rage, and what does it say about heaven's justice?
body: The Muse is asked for 'causes' (causas), and the line that closes the invocation is one of the most quoted in Latin. 'Celestial spirits' are the minds of the gods; irae, 'angers', is plural, suggesting repeated or many-sided outbursts. The question echoes, without solving, philosophical objections to the passionate gods of myth (Epicurean and Stoic thinkers denied that gods could feel anger). Juno's resentment, her 'unforgetful anger' (memorem iram, 1.4), opens the action at 1.34-49, and the poem ends with another act of anger, Aeneas' killing of Turnus (12.946-7). Readers have long debated whether the Aeneid finally justifies the suffering it narrates or leaves the question open; this line is where that debate begins.

title: Carthage, Juno's city
greek: urbs antiqua fuit ... Karthago
short: Carthage, the Phoenician city in North Africa, was Rome's great enemy in the three Punic Wars; Virgil makes it Juno's favourite and Rome's destined victim.
body: Carthage (Punic Qart-hadasht, 'new city', hence Mackail's 'New Carthage' at 1.366) was founded by settlers from Tyre in Phoenicia, traditionally in the late ninth century BC. 'Over against Italy' marks it as Rome's rival across the sea. Juno favoured it even above Samos, one of her great cult centres (the Carthaginians worshipped a goddess, Tanit, whom Romans identified with Juno). Virgil's first readers knew the end of the story: Rome fought Carthage in three Punic Wars (264-146 BC) and destroyed it in 146 BC, the 'destroyer of Libya' (excidio Libyae) of 1.22. So Virgil writes the Punic Wars into the poem's foundations: Juno's hatred of Troy is also a mythical cause of the historical enmity, which Dido will curse into being at 4.622-9. 'There was' (fuit) has been read as a quiet hint that the city no longer stands.

title: Juno's grievances: Paris and Ganymede
greek: iudicium Paridis spretaeque iniuria formae ... et rapti Ganymedis honores
short: Juno hates the Trojans for the judgment of Paris, which slighted her beauty, for their descent from Jupiter's affair, and for Ganymede's promotion to heaven.
body: Juno, 'daughter of Saturn' (Saturnia, her standard title), has three old wounds. At the judgment of Paris the Trojan prince awarded the golden apple to Venus rather than to Juno or Minerva, an insult to her beauty. The 'hated race' are the Trojans, descended from Dardanus, son of Jupiter by Electra, so a reminder of her husband's infidelity (Page and Conington explain it this way). Ganymede, a Trojan prince, was carried off to Olympus to be Jupiter's cupbearer and favourite, and his 'dignities' displaced Juno's daughter Hebe. To these personal grudges Virgil adds the political one of Carthage (1.12-22). The motivation is Homeric in kind (Hera hates Troy in the Iliad, and Il. 24.25-30 is the only Homeric mention of Paris' judgment), but Virgil sets it out as a catalogue of injured honour that keeps her anger alive long after Troy's fall.

anchor: Such work was it to found
title: 'Such work was it to found the Roman people'
greek: tantae molis erat Romanam condere gentem
short: A single line summing up the first section: Rome's foundation cost immense effort, and the poem is about that labour.
body: Moles means a great mass, and then the effort needed to move a great mass. Page translates 'of so great effort' or 'so great a task it was'. The line closes the proem with a spondaic weight that imitates the struggle it describes, and it gives the poem its moral centre: Roman greatness is not easy but is paid for in suffering, much of it borne by the defeated and by those sacrificed along the way (Dido, Turnus, Pallas, Creusa). The verb condere, 'to found', literally 'to put together' or 'to store', recurs at key points, and Roman readers would hear in 'the Roman people' (gentem) the whole national community of their own day. Compare Aeneas' own words 'Through chequered fortunes ... we steer for Latium' at 1.204-6.

title: Teucrians, Dardanians, Phrygians: names for the Trojans
greek: Teucrorum ... regem
short: Virgil calls the Trojans by several ancestral names: Teucrians (from Teucer), Dardanians (from Dardanus), Phrygians (from the region), and Aeneadae (Aeneas' men).
body: 'Teucrians' (Teucri) come from Teucer, an early king of the Troad whose daughter married Dardanus; 'Dardanians' from Dardanus himself, son of Jupiter and founder of the royal line (in Virgil he comes originally from Italy, 3.167-8); 'Phrygians' from the region of Asia Minor around Troy, a name that could carry a sneer of eastern softness in Roman mouths (Iarbas and Numanus use it so at 4.215 and 9.599-620); 'Ilian' from Ilium, the city named after Ilus. Aeneas' followers are also 'Aeneadae', 'sons of Aeneas' (1.157), a word Lucretius used of the Romans in his first line. Do not confuse the ancestral Teucer with Teucer son of Telamon, the Greek archer who visits Sidon at 1.619. Juno's sneering 'Teucrian king' is the first of these names in the poem.

title: Ajax son of Oileus
greek: unius ob noxam et furias Aiacis Oilei
short: The 'lesser' Ajax, who dragged Cassandra from Minerva's temple; the goddess wrecked the Greek fleet on its way home and impaled him on a rock.
body: There were two Greek heroes named Ajax; this one, son of Oileus and leader of the Locrians, is distinguished from Telamonian Ajax by his father's name (Oilei is a patronymic genitive, as Conington explains). At the sack of Troy he dragged Cassandra away from Minerva's altar (2.403-6), and Minerva (Pallas) took vengeance on the whole Greek fleet. Juno's complaint is that a lesser goddess may destroy a whole navy for one man's 'madness' (furias), while she, queen of the gods, cannot finish off one small people. Her version of Ajax's death, struck with Jupiter's thunderbolt and fixed on a crag, differs from Homer's, where Poseidon drowns him for boasting (Od. 4.499-511); Conington discusses the variants. The episode is a Virgilian 'ring': Cassandra's dragging is shown in Book 2, its punishment told first here.

title: Aeolus and the cave of the winds
greek: Aeoliam venit ... rex Aeolus
short: Aeolus, keeper of the winds, rules them in a mountain prison; Virgil turns Homer's genial host of Odyssey 10 into a political image of controlled violence.
body: In Homer (Od. 10.1-27) Aeolus lives on a floating island and gives Odysseus the winds tied in a bag. Virgil places him in the volcanic Aeolian islands north of Sicily and makes him a gaoler: the winds 'rage indignant' in their cave, held down by a mountain and by a 'king' who knows when to tighten and slacken the reins. The language is political (imperio premit, 'keeps under royal dominion'; foedere certo, 'by certain law'), and readers have long seen in it Virgil's recurring theme of disorder held in check by authority, which the Neptune simile at 1.148-53 makes explicit. Juno's bribe and Aeolus' release of the winds set off the storm, a set piece modelled on Odyssey 5.291-332 (Poseidon's storm against Odysseus). The 'father of gods and king of men' is a Homeric formula for Zeus (pater andron te theon te).

title: 'Thrice and four times happy': Aeneas' first words
greek: o terque quaterque beati
short: Aeneas' first speech, a wish that he had died at Troy, translates Odysseus' cry in the storm of Odyssey 5 and introduces the hero in despair.
body: The first time Aeneas appears he is chilled with fear and wishes himself dead. The speech closely adapts Odyssey 5.306-12, where Odysseus, caught in Poseidon's storm, says the Greeks who died at Troy were 'three and four times blessed' (trismakares kai tetrakis). Virgil changes the point of view: Aeneas envies the Trojans who died 'before their fathers' faces' defending their city, and he names Diomedes ('son of Tydeus'), who almost killed him in Iliad 5.297-317, Hector killed by Achilles ('Aeacides', grandson of Aeacus), Sarpedon, and the river Simois rolling armour and bodies (Il. 12.22-3, 21.218-20). The opening portrait of a hero who longs for death, not glory, sets the tone of a poem that is preoccupied with loss.

anchor: one reverend for goodness and service
title: The statesman simile
greek: ac veluti magno in populo cum saepe coorta est seditio ... tum pietate gravem ac meritis si forte virum quem conspexere, silent
short: The poem's first simile compares Neptune calming the sea to a respected statesman quelling a riot: nature is explained by politics, not the other way round.
body: Homeric similes usually illustrate human action by nature (a warrior like a lion). Virgil reverses this: a storm at sea is like a civil riot, and Neptune is like 'one reverend for goodness and service' (pietate gravem ac meritis) whose words calm the crowd. Conington glosses pietate as the general discharge of duty and meritis as services to the state. The image of furor ('madness lends arms', furor arma ministrat) mastered by authority speaks directly to Romans who had lived through decades of civil war, and readers have often thought of a Roman statesman such as Augustus (the simile does not name him). It also anticipates the end of Jupiter's speech, where 'Fury' is chained (1.294-6).

title: 'One day it will please us to remember even this'
greek: forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit
short: Aeneas' speech of comfort, modelled on Odysseus, ends with the most famous consolation in Latin; the narrator then shows that he does not believe it himself.
body: Aeneas rallies his men by recalling dangers survived, Scylla and the Cyclops (both told at length in Book 3), as Odysseus does at Odyssey 12.208-12 ('these too, I think, we shall one day remember'). The line forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit has become proverbial. But Virgil immediately adds what Homer does not: 'sick with deep distress he feigns hope on his face, and keeps his anguish hidden deep in his breast' (spem vultu simulat, premit altum corde dolorem, 1.209). Page points out the chiastic order of that line, hope and face set against heart and grief. The gap between the leader's public face and his private feeling is a defining trait of Virgil's hero and of the burden of leadership.

title: Jupiter's prophecy: 'empire without end'
greek: his ego nec metas rerum nec tempora pono: imperium sine fine dedi
short: Jupiter reveals the 'secret records of fate': from Aeneas to Romulus to Caesar, Rome will receive power without limit of space or time.
body: This speech is the first of the poem's three great views of Roman history (with the parade of heroes in 6.756-892 and the shield in 8.626-728). Jupiter counts out the years: three for Aeneas in Latium, thirty for Ascanius at Lavinium and Alba Longa, three hundred for the Alban kings until Ilia (Rhea Silvia) bears Romulus and Remus to Mars. Then he removes the counting altogether: 'I set no bounds in space or time; I have given empire without end.' Virgil's readers knew the claim as Augustan ideology. Conington sees the following line, Rome as 'lords of the world, the gowned race' (Romanos rerum dominos gentemque togatam), as a stock grand phrase; the toga marked the civilian Roman citizen. Notice too the promise that Juno 'shall change to better counsels', fulfilled only in Book 12 (12.791-842).

title: Ascanius-Iulus and the Julian family
greek: at puer Ascanius, cui nunc cognomen Iulo additur (Ilus erat, dum res stetit Ilia regno)
short: Virgil explains Aeneas' son's second name, Iulus, as derived from Ilus and Ilium; through it the Julian clan of Julius Caesar and Augustus claimed descent from Aeneas and Venus.
body: Ascanius is the name of Aeneas' son in Homer (Il. 2.862 has an Ascanius, though not his son) and in Greek tradition. 'Iulus' was the name the Julii, the family of Julius Caesar and his adopted son Octavian (Augustus), claimed as their ancestor. Virgil connects it with Ilus, founder of Ilium, so that the Roman family name reaches back to Troy itself; the etymology is poetic, not scientific. Livy, writing at the same time, admits uncertainty whether Iulus was Ascanius or another son of Aeneas (Livy 1.3.2). Throughout the poem Virgil moves between the two names, using 'Iulus' when the Roman future is in view. Through Iulus the Julian family could present itself as descended from Venus herself.

title: 'A Caesar shall arise': Julius or Augustus?
greek: nascetur pulchra Troianus origine Caesar ... Iulius, a magno demissum nomen Iulo
short: Jupiter predicts a 'Trojan Caesar' who will be deified; scholars disagree whether he means Julius Caesar or Augustus (who also bore the name Julius).
body: The prophecy names a 'Caesar of Trojan origin' called 'Julius', whose empire is bounded by Ocean and whose fame by the stars, who will be received in heaven 'loaded with Eastern spoils', and in whose time wars will end. Page argues that Augustus is meant: Octavian became C. Julius Caesar Octavianus on his adoption, and the name Julius is used to mark his descent from Iulus; the Eastern spoils fit his triumph of 29 BC after Actium and Egypt, and the closing of the gates of war follows. Others have held that Julius Caesar, deified after 44 BC, is meant, since the comet of 44 and his deification answer 'welcome to heaven'. The ambiguity may be deliberate, binding both Caesars into one Trojan line. Either way the speech brings the myth down to Virgil's own present.

title: The gates of war (temple of Janus)
greek: dirae ferro et compagibus artis claudentur Belli portae; Furor impius intus ...
short: The doors of the shrine of Janus in the Forum stood open in war and were closed in peace; Augustus closed them in 29 BC, an event this prophecy celebrates.
body: Roman custom held that the doors of the small temple of Janus Geminus near the Forum should be shut only when Rome was at peace on all fronts. They had been closed only twice before Augustus, who boasts in the Res Gestae (13) that they were closed three times in his principate, the first in 29 BC. Virgil describes the ritual of opening them in detail at 7.607-22. Here the shut gates imprison 'Fury' (Furor impius, 'godless Madness'), chained with a hundred brazen knots and roaring with bloody mouth, an image of civil war defeated. Readers have noticed that the poem's last act, Aeneas killing Turnus 'set on fire by fury' (furiis accensus, 12.946), sits uneasily with this vision. Faith (Fides), Vesta and Quirinus with his brother Remus (Romulus deified) giving laws signal a return to old Roman virtue and an end to fratricide.

title: Venus disguised as a huntress
greek: virginis os habitumque gerens et virginis arma Spartanae
short: Venus meets her son disguised as a Tyrian huntress, a scene modelled on Athena's disguised meetings with Odysseus, and reveals herself only as she leaves.
body: Disguised divine guides are Homeric: Athena meets Odysseus as a young girl at Phaeacia (Od. 7.19-77) and as a shepherd on Ithaca (Od. 13.221-440). Venus appears as a huntress like a Spartan girl or the Thracian huntress Harpalyce; Page notes that Virgil seems to have statues of Diana in mind. She tells Aeneas Dido's history and shows him an augury of twelve swans (1.393-400). Only when she turns away do her rosy neck, ambrosial hair and gait reveal the goddess: 'the godhead was manifest in her tread' (vera incessu patuit dea, 1.405). Aeneas' reproach, 'Thou also merciless!', and his complaint that he may never clasp her hand, show the distance between mortal son and divine mother, a theme that recurs when he cannot embrace Creusa's ghost (2.792) or his father's shade (6.700).

title: Dido, Sychaeus and Pygmalion
greek: huic coniunx Sychaeus erat ... Pygmalion
short: Venus tells how Dido's brother Pygmalion, king of Tyre, murdered her husband Sychaeus for his gold, and how Dido fled with the treasure to found Carthage.
body: Dido (also called Elissa in other sources) was a Tyrian princess. Her husband Sychaeus, 'wealthiest in lands of the Phoenicians', was killed at the altar by her brother Pygmalion (not the sculptor of Ovid's tale), and his ghost appeared to her in a dream, revealing the crime and buried treasure. The story, also told by the historian Justin (18.4-6, from Timaeus), presents Dido as an energetic leader: 'a woman leads the work' (dux femina facti). Virgil makes her loyalty to Sychaeus central: her vow of faithfulness to him (4.24-9) is what her love for Aeneas will break. Sychaeus' ghost and Dido's flight anticipate Aeneas' own dream of Hector and flight from Troy in Book 2; the two exiles mirror each other. Conington notes that the quantity of the first syllable of Sychaeus' name varies in the poets (Servius: short by nature, lengthened here by the licence allowed to proper names).

title: Byrsa and the bull's hide
greek: mercatique solum, facti de nomine Byrsam, taurino quantum possent circumdare tergo
short: The citadel of Carthage, Byrsa, was explained by the story that Dido bought as much land as a bull's hide could cover, then cut the hide into strips.
body: Greek byrsa means 'hide'. The story ran that the settlers bought from the Africans as much ground as an oxhide would enclose, and then cut it into thin strips to surround a whole hill. Conington and Page both explain the name as a Greek misunderstanding of a Phoenician word for 'citadel' (Bosra; compare Hebrew Bozrah), which Greeks reinterpreted through their own word and then explained with an aetiological tale. Virgil's phrase 'called thence' (facti de nomine) signals that he is telling an origin story. The trick also characterises Dido as resourceful, and it is a small instance of the cunning ascribed to Phoenicians that Venus later fears in 'the double-tongued race of Tyre' (1.661).

title: The Penates (household gods)
greek: sum pius Aeneas, raptos qui ex hoste penatis classe veho mecum
short: The Penates were gods of the household store and, by extension, of the Roman state; Aeneas' rescue of Troy's Penates is the core of his pietas.
body: The Penates (from penus, the store-cupboard) were guardian spirits of the household, worshipped with the Lares at the family hearth. Rome also had public Penates, kept with Vesta's sacred things and connected by tradition with those Aeneas brought from Troy to Lavinium, where Roman magistrates sacrificed to them. Aeneas introduces himself by this act: 'I am pious Aeneas, who carry with me in my fleet the Penates rescued from the enemy'. To modern ears the self-praise ('my fame is known high in heaven') sounds odd, but it follows Odysseus' self-introduction at Od. 9.19-20. Hector entrusts the gods to Aeneas at 2.293-7, and in Book 3 they appear to him in a dream (3.147-71). Mackail's 'household gods' always renders penates.

title: The bee simile: Carthage being built
greek: qualis apes aestate nova per florea rura exercet sub sole labor
short: The Carthaginians building their city are like bees in early summer, an image of ordered communal work that Virgil had developed in Georgics 4.
body: Aeneas looks down on Carthage under construction: walls, citadel, harbours, a theatre, laws, magistrates and a senate. Virgil compares the workers to bees, reusing lines from his own Georgics (4.162-9) where the bee community is an image of an ideal state. Behind it also lies Iliad 2.87-90, the Greek army pouring out like bees. Aeneas' cry 'Happy they whose city already rises!' (o fortunati, quorum iam moenia surgunt, 1.437) expresses his longing for the city he has not yet founded. Some readers see irony, since Carthage is the city Rome will destroy and the work will stop when Dido falls in love (4.86-9); others stress the Roman features of Dido's city.

title: Sunt lacrimae rerum: the Trojan murals
greek: sunt hic etiam sua praemia laudi; sunt lacrimae rerum et mentem mortalia tangunt
short: Seeing the Trojan War painted on Juno's temple, Aeneas weeps: 'there are tears for things, and mortal matters touch the mind', one of Latin's most famous and debated lines.
body: The temple paintings are an ekphrasis (a description of a work of art) showing scenes from the Trojan War: Rhesus' horses stolen before they could drink from the Xanthus (Iliad 10), Troilus dragged by his chariot, the Trojan women offering a robe to the hostile Pallas (Il. 6.286-311), Hector's body ransomed (Il. 24), Memnon, and the Amazon Penthesilea. Aeneas reads in them sympathy: 'here too merit has its reward; there are tears for things (lacrimae rerum), and mortal fortunes touch the heart'. Rerum is open: the genitive can mean tears shed for things or tears belonging to the world itself, and the line is often quoted in a general sense never quite meant. Aeneas 'feeds his soul on an empty picture' (pictura pascit inani, 1.464). Readers debate whether the Carthaginians meant the paintings as sympathy or as a monument of Greek victory in Juno's temple.

title: Dido like Diana
greek: qualis in Eurotae ripis aut per iuga Cynthi exercet Diana choros
short: Dido's entrance is compared to Diana leading her nymphs, adapting the Homeric simile for Nausicaa; ancient critics already argued whether it fits.
body: The simile adapts Odyssey 6.102-9, where Nausicaa among her maidens is like Artemis on the mountains, and Leto rejoices in her daughter. Eurotas is the river of Sparta, Cynthus the hill on Delos where Diana (Artemis) and Apollo were born, and Latona (Leto) their mother. Already in antiquity Valerius Probus, reported by Aulus Gellius (9.9.12-17), judged Virgil's version inferior, since it suits a girl at play better than a queen at work. Conington discusses the objection and finds the comparison less appropriate to Dido walking among her lords than to Nausicaa. Others answer that the image is pointed: Diana is a virgin goddess and Dido a widow vowed to chastity, and the simile reverses itself at 4.143-50, where Aeneas is compared to Apollo, Diana's brother.

title: Hesperia, Oenotria, Italy
greek: est locus, Hesperiam Grai cognomine dicunt ... Oenotri coluere viri; nunc fama minores Italiam dixisse ducis de nomine gentem
short: Ilioneus names the Trojans' goal with three names: Greek 'Hesperia' (western land), 'Oenotria', and 'Italy', said to come from a leader called Italus.
body: Hesperia means 'the land of evening', the west as seen from Greece. The Oenotrians were early inhabitants of southern Italy; the name was linked with oinos, 'wine'. 'Italy' was explained by a king Italus (Aristotle, Politics 1329b, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus 1.35 report the tradition). The same four lines recur almost word for word when the Penates speak to Aeneas at 3.163-6; Virgil sometimes repeats lines, in the manner of Homer, and here the repetition makes the destination sound like a formula of fate. The broken line after 'Thither lay our course' (hic cursus fuit, 1.534) is one of the half-lines left incomplete at Virgil's death, which Mackail marks with dots.

title: 'Goddess-born' (nate dea)
greek: nate dea
short: A formal mode of address for Aeneas, son of Venus, used by friends, prophets and gods; it marks both his divine status and the weight of his destiny.
body: Nate dea, literally 'born of a goddess', is Virgil's equivalent of Homeric forms of address such as diogenes, 'sprung from Zeus', and of the stress on Achilles' mother Thetis. Achates uses it here; it recurs in Hector's ghost (2.289), Helenus (3.374, 435) and Anchises' shade. It reminds readers that Aeneas is a demigod whose goal is fixed by fate, but Virgil often places it where Aeneas is at his most human and vulnerable. Dido uses the variant 'goddess-born' at 1.615 when she first wonders at his fortunes.

title: Aeneas revealed: the ivory simile
greek: quale manus addunt ebori decus, aut ubi flavo argentum Pariusve lapis circumdatur auro
short: When the cloud parts, Venus has made her son shine like a god; the simile of craftsmen adorning ivory comes from Athena's beautifying of Odysseus.
body: Venus had hidden Aeneas and Achates in a cloud (1.411-14), as Athena hides Odysseus in mist on his way to the Phaeacian palace (Od. 7.14-17, 139-45). Now the cloud melts and Aeneas stands 'like a god in face and shoulders', with youthful bloom and joyful eyes. The simile translates Odyssey 6.229-35 (repeated at 23.156-62), where Athena pours grace on Odysseus 'as when a craftsman overlays silver with gold'. Virgil adds ivory and Parian marble, the white stone of Paros used in sculpture. The beauty is a divine gift and part of Venus' plan; it is the first step in Dido's falling in love. Note the irony that Aeneas' first words begin 'I whom you seek am here', a dramatic self-revelation like Odysseus' at Od. 24.321.

title: 'Not ignorant of ill'
greek: non ignara mali miseris succurrere disco
short: Dido's welcome rests on shared suffering: having known misfortune, she has learned to help the wretched. Her sympathy is the beginning of her tragedy.
body: Dido's line is one of the poem's most quoted sentences on compassion. 'Not ignorant' (a litotes, saying something by denying its opposite) echoes Aeneas' own 'for not now nor aforetime are we ignorant of ill' at 1.198 (neque enim ignari sumus ante malorum), so that the two exiles speak the same language before they meet. Dido offers equal citizenship: 'Trojan and Tyrian shall be held by me in even balance' (Tros Tyriusque mihi nullo discrimine agetur, 1.574). The generosity of her hospitality makes Aeneas' departure in Book 4 the more painful, and the gods' manipulation of her (Venus' and Cupid's plot follows immediately) the more troubling.

title: Cupid disguised as Ascanius
greek: Cytherea novas artes ... ut faciem mutatus et ora Cupido pro dulci Ascanio veniat
short: Venus sends Cupid in Ascanius' likeness to inflame Dido; the real boy is laid asleep in her groves at Idalium in Cyprus, among fragrant marjoram.
body: Venus fears Juno's influence in Carthage and the 'double-tongued' Tyrians, and so ensures that Dido is held by passion. Cupid ('winged Love', Amor) takes the shape of Ascanius, sits in Dido's lap at the banquet and breathes into her a 'hidden fire'. The scene adapts Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3.111-66 and 275-98, where Aphrodite sends Eros to make Medea love Jason. Idalium and Cythera are cult places of Venus; amaracus is sweet marjoram. Venus calls Cupid scornful of 'the mighty father's Typhoïan shafts' (tela Typhoea, 1.665), the thunderbolts with which Jupiter struck the giant Typhoeus: love is stronger than Jupiter's weapons. Readers have noted how this divine plot reduces Dido's responsibility for what follows, and how it compromises Venus.

title: Hospitium: Jupiter the god of guests
greek: Iuppiter, hospitibus nam te dare iura loquuntur
short: Dido's libation to Jupiter as protector of guests and hosts invokes hospitium, the sacred bond of guest-friendship, and the banquet follows the Homeric pattern of the hero's reception.
body: Hospitium, like Greek xenia, was a binding relationship between guest and host protected by Jupiter Hospitalis (Zeus Xenios). Dido calls for a heavy jewelled cup of her ancestors, pours a libation (a drink-offering, poured on the table), touches it with her lips and passes it to Bitias. She prays that the day be joyful for Tyrians and Trojans and remembered by descendants. The scene follows the Homeric sequence at the Phaeacian court (Od. 7-8): washing of hands, food and wine, then song, then the stranger's story. The irony is that this bond will be broken; Dido later accuses Aeneas of betraying it, calling him 'guest' instead of 'husband' (hospes, 4.323). Ilioneus had already appealed to it in his plea against Carthaginian hostility (1.539-41).

title: Iopas' song of the universe
greek: cithara crinitus Iopas personat aurata, docuit quem maximus Atlas
short: Dido's bard sings not of heroes but of the cosmos (moon, sun, origins of life, stars and seasons), a philosophical song in the manner of Lucretius.
body: Homeric banquets have bards (Demodocus in Odyssey 8 sings of Troy). Virgil's Iopas, taught by Atlas (the Titan who holds up the sky and was associated with astronomy), sings natural philosophy: the wandering moon, eclipses, the origins of men, beasts, rain and fire, the constellations Arcturus, the rainy Hyades and the twin Triones (the Bears), and why winter days are short. Conington compares Virgil's own wish to be taught such things by the Muses (Georgics 2.475-82) and the cosmological songs of Orpheus (Apollonius 1.496-511) and Silenus (Eclogue 6.31-40). Page calls Iopas Virgil's ideal of poetry. The lines on winter suns are repeated from Georgics 2.481-2, and the stars recur at 3.516.

title: 'The seventh summer': the chronology of the wanderings
greek: nam te iam septima portat omnibus errantem terris et fluctibus aestas
short: Dido says Aeneas has been wandering for seven summers; yet a year later in Book 5 the same phrase is used, a famous inconsistency left by the unrevised poem.
body: The line sets the frame for Books 2-3: Aeneas will tell the fall of Troy and seven years of wandering. But at 5.626 Iris (disguised as Beroe) also says 'the seventh summer is now turning since Troy's fall', although Book 4 has taken the story through a winter in Carthage. Commentators have explained this by assuming that Virgil did not live to revise the poem (he died in 19 BC with the Aeneid unfinished; the half-lines are another sign). Conington, on the chronology of Book 3, works out the years in Thrace, Delos and Crete. Students should treat the poem's chronology as approximate, though seven is also a conventional round number for long wanderings, as for Odysseus with Calypso (Od. 7.259).
